newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: MINISTER SAYS BE REALISTIC ABOUT GLOBAL WARMING
Environment minister Robert Hill says the Federal Government is not prepared to accept legally binding limits on Greenhouse gas emissions because it could cost Australian jobs.
U.S. President Bill Clinton called on countries to accept legally binding limits on Greenhouse gas emissions during his Australian visit.
But Senator Hill told a National Forum on Australia's changing climate, the Government has a responsibility to grow the economy and produce jobs as well as improving the Greenhouse performance.
He says the government is committed to tackling the Greenhouse problem but any binding agreement could damage Australian industry.
BLACK DEATHS REPORT BRINGS MORE CRITICISM
The ATSIC chair, Lois O'Donoghue, has accused Australian Governments of regarding indigenous lives as less valuable than others.
She was speaking at the the launch of a report into the 1989 Black Deaths in Custody Royal Commission.

The report, by ATSIC Social Justice Commissioner, Mick Dodson, reveals many of the Royal Commission's 339 recommendations were breached in relation to the 96 Aboriginal deaths in custody that have occurred since.
The average was eight-and-a-half recommendationms breached, but Queensland, with 13 recommendations breached, was the worst state.
Mr Dodson says the situation is disturbing.
The 500 page report makes 76 recommendations.
COFF HARBOUR DECLARED A NATURAL DISASTER AREA
New South Wales Premier, Bob Carr, has announced a disaster relief package for Coffs Harbour, which was devastated by flash floods at the weekend.
The package will fund repairs to local government infrastructure, including roads and bridges.
Businesses will also be able to apply for low interest loans, but many inner-city shopowners say they'll be forced to close because of the floods, the worst for over 30 years.

The city has officially been designated a natural disaster area. The State Government's pledged A$76,000 to the city council to upgrade its flood plain management program to try to ensure similar flooding doesn't occur again.
WORKERS "RIPPED OFF" THROUGH PAYROLL SYSTEM
A business advisory group says many Australians are not getting the right pay because of the country's complicated payroll system.

The Association for Payroll Specialists says Australia has the most complicated payroll and taxation system in the world, making it impossible for most of its 8.5 million workers to know if their wages are correct.
Director Ken Low says workers are being ripped off and the complexities are costing business millions of dollars a year.
He says the procedures, including industrial relations, should be standardised around the country.
RAIL PLAN HEADING FOR SENATE BUFFERS
Opposition to the Federal Government's plans to sell its national rail operations is growing, with a Government Senator the latest to express concern.
Jeannie Ferris says she has a number of concerns about the planned sale of the Australian National Passenger Services and the National Rail Corporation, especially job losses.
Senator Ferris' comments come after Federal Transport Minister, John Sharp, hailed the plan as a renaissance for Australian rail.
But Greens Senator, Dee Margetts, says the Government shouldn't be hiving off its rail responsibilities.
And Democrats Senator, Andrew Murray, says his party's concerned about what he called "the automatic charge towards privatisation".
WEATHER KEY TO MOZZIE PROBLEMS
An expert on mosquito-borne diseases says this year's mozzie problem will depend on the weather.
Sydney University medical entomologist, Professor Richard Russell, says New South Wales had a wet spring, which would have set the scene for a bad mosquito season.
But Professor Russell says the weather has also been cool, which has prevented the development of some populations.
Mosquito experts from all over the world are meeting on Queensland's Gold Coast this week for a conference to discuss mozzie control, and the treatment of mosquito-borne diseases.
COMMANDER'S CONCERNS ABOUT BLACKHAWK EXERCISES
An Army commanding officer has told the Blackhawk inquiry he instituted a safety margin to deal with his concerns about a lack of experience among air crews.
Lieutenant Colonel Tony Fraser, is commander of the Townsville-based Fifth Aviation unit, which lost four air crew in June's mid-air collision between two Blackhawks.
Colonel Fraser said he found out only after the accident that the helicopters had been flying in a formation he considered dangerous.
He said when he took over control of the regiment in late 1995, he was aware of cultural problems associated with counter terrorism exercises, which were dangerous.
The inquiry has today begun hearings in Sydney.
DEMOCRATS NOT SURPRISED BY INDUSTRIAL ACTION THREATS
The Australian Democrats say they're not too surprised at threats by the ACTU of widespread industrial action if the Government attacks the power of the Maritime Union, using the new industrial law.
Waterfront workers have already had one strike against last week's passage through the Senate of the Workplace Relations Bill, especially its banning of secondary boycotts.
Democrats Senator, Andrew Murray, who was instrumental in getting the legislation passed, says there'll inevitably be some shoving and pushing as the new law comes into effect.
He says it's only natural unions will seek to maximise their position, but predicts the whole situation will settle down.
